acolyte

AK-uh-lyte · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Acolyte is a devoted follower, assistant, or attendant who serves a leader or cause loyally and up close.

The aging philosopher rarely traveled anywhere without a small circle of acolytes eager to record his every word.

Example

Within a year of joining the startup, the intern had become one of the founder's most loyal acolytes, defending every decision he made.

Being a devoted, almost admiring follower or attendant of someone is exactly what acolyte describes.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

follower: A follower is anyone who supports a leader or movement, even from a distance -- one face in a crowd. An acolyte is far closer: a devoted assistant who personally serves the leader, often so admiringly that the devotion looks uncritical.

devotee: A devotee is intensely enthusiastic about a cause, an art, or a person -- a devotee of jazz, of chess, of a teacher. An acolyte turns that enthusiasm into service: attending the leader up close and helping with the daily work.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

critic: a person who points out faults or disagrees

rival: a person competing against another

Where it sits · how deep the devotion runs

protege → acolyte → disciple

protege vs. acolyte: Protege is milder than acolyte: a protege simply learns the ropes under a mentor's guidance, while an acolyte goes further, devotedly serving the leader and the cause itself.

disciple vs. acolyte: Disciple is stronger than acolyte: an acolyte devotedly assists a leader, but a disciple commits more deeply, memorizing the master's teachings word for word and spreading them everywhere.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — a-: together, with (Greek -- the 'joining' a- at the start of akolouthos)

Root — colyte: path, road (from Greek keleuthos, 'path,' reshaped through Latin acolytus)

Put it together: Acolyte comes from Greek akolouthos, 'follower, one who accompanies': a- ('together, with') + colyte (from keleuthos, 'path,' reshaped through Latin acolytus) -- someone walking the same path together with the person they follow. The word entered English through its use for a church assistant who helped a priest, and later broadened to mean any devoted follower.

Where it comes from: Picture an acolyte the way Greek built the word: a- ('together, with') plus keleuthos ('path') -- someone walking the same road as the person they follow. English first used it for a church assistant who helped a priest, then widened it to any devoted follower.

Word Building

Word Choice

Acolyte often carries a faintly critical or ironic edge in modern use -- describing someone as a leader's acolyte can suggest their devotion is a little too uncritical or unquestioning, not just loyal.
